summary: Defines a URN namespace for 3GPP2 and a namespace-specific string for the Mobile Equipment Identity (MEID), a 15-hexadecimal-digit identifier that uniquely identifies a mobile device.

plainLanguage.summary: Every phone has its own ID number. This gives that number a standard web-style name format.

subtitle: Standardized web format for unique cell phone IDs

tldr.problem: 3GPP2 mobile devices use a different equipment ID format (MEID) than 3GPP devices (IMEI), but there was no standard URN namespace to represent MEIDs in protocols and databases.
tldr.mechanism: This document registers the '3gpp2' URN namespace with a namespace-specific string for MEID, defining the syntax as 'urn:3gpp2:meid:ManufacturerCode-SerialNumber' where both are hexadecimal digits, matching 14 of the 15-digit MEID (the check digit is omitted).
tldr.outcome: The 3GPP2 MEID URN enables protocols to identify mobile equipment in a standard, interoperable way, used in applications like SIP (RFC 5626) and emergency services where device identification is necessary.

today: RFC 8464 registers the 3gpp2 URN namespace with IANA. RFC 8465 (published at the same time) specifies how the MEID URN is used as an Instance ID in SIP. The MEID URN is now used by applications and protocols that need to identify 3GPP2 mobile equipment in a standardized way.

sections.title: Mobile Device Identification and the MEID
sections.content:
Mobile devices need unique identifiers for network management, billing, and operations. 3GPP (primarily used by GSM/LTE networks) identifies devices with an IMEI (International Mobile station Equipment Identity). 3GPP2 (used by CDMA networks) identifies devices with an MEID (Mobile Equipment Identity). The MEID is a 15-hexadecimal-digit number: 8 digits for the manufacturer code, 6 digits for the serial number within that manufacturer, and 1 digit for a check digit used in inventory operations (but not transmitted).

While 3GPP/3GPP2 dual-mode devices can use IMEI (RFC 7254 defines an IMEI URN), single-mode 3GPP2 devices require a different approach. The MEID URN enables 3GPP2 devices to be identified in internet protocols using a standard, hierarchical URN format, fulfilling a 3GPP2 requirement and enabling applications like SIP and emergency services to work consistently across device types.
sections.plainLanguage: CDMA phones have a different ID format than GSM phones. This creates a standard way to write those IDs so internet programs can recognize them.

sections.title: MEID Structure and Components
sections.content:
The MEID is a 15-hexadecimal-digit number with three components. The manufacturer code (8 digits) identifies the device maker and is assigned from ranges allocated to each manufacturer. The serial number (6 digits) uniquely identifies each device within the manufacturer code. The check digit (1 digit) is used for integrity checking in inventory systems (e.g., when reading MEIDs from barcodes) but is not transmitted by the device and not used in the URN.

The manufacturer code and serial number are permanently stored in the device and never change, even if the device is resold or completely reloaded with software. This permanent identity enables device tracking and management throughout its lifetime. The MEID is typically printed on the device box, sometimes under the battery, and can be retrieved by dialing *#06# on most CDMA phones.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID has three parts: who made it (8 digits), which one it is (6 digits), and a check number (1 digit). The first two stay the same forever; the check digit is just for catching typos.

sections.title: URN Format and Namespace Registration
sections.content:
The 3gpp2 URN namespace is registered with the IANA per RFC 8141. MEIDs are represented with the syntax: urn:3gpp2:meid:ManufacturerCode-SerialNumber. For example, urn:3gpp2:meid:A04B0D56-02A7E3 represents a device made by the manufacturer code A04B0D56 with serial number 02A7E3.

Only the first 14 hexadecimal digits (manufacturer code and serial number) are used in the URN; the check digit is omitted. The namespace allows for future expansion; 3GPP2 may define other types of NSS under the 3gpp2 NID in the future. All components are in uppercase hexadecimal (A-F and 0-9), and the check digit is never included in the URN representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is simple: start with 'urn:3gpp2:meid:' then the 8-digit manufacturer code, a dash, and the 6-digit serial number. That's the complete web address for a phone ID.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Implications
sections.content:
The MEID is not a security capability. It is easily accessible (printed on the box or device, retrievable by dialing *#06#) and MUST NOT be used as proof of ownership or as a secret authentication factor. Unfortunately, some applications and service providers misuse MEIDs for authorization, a practice this RFC explicitly discourages. Anyone with brief physical access to a phone or its box can obtain the MEID.

Since the MEID is permanently tied to the device and never changes with ownership, it MUST NOT be used as a user identifier or user address. Using it as such could result in messages intended for the previous owner being received by the new owner, or the new owner accessing the previous owner's services and data. The MEID should be treated as personally identifiable information; protocols carrying MEID URNs SHOULD use hop-by-hop encryption and SHOULD preferably use end-to-end encryption to prevent tracking and surveillance.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone ID isn't secret; anyone can find it. So don't use it to prove someone owns a phone. Also, since it stays the same when a phone changes hands, don't use it to identify who owns the phone.

data.title: MEID URN Format
data.code:
urn:3gpp2:meid:A04B0D56-02A7E3
  |
  +-- Namespace (3gpp2)
  |    
  +---- Type (meid)      
  |      
  +------ Manufacturer Code: A04B0D56
  |       
  +------ Serial Number: 02A7E3
